title: Of cannibals
paragraphs: When King Pyrrhus invaded Italy, after surveying the order of the army the Romans had sent out to meet him, he said: "I do not know what kind of barbarians these may be" — for so the Greeks called all other nations — "but the disposition of this army that I see before me has nothing barbarous in it." The Greeks said as much of the army Flaminius brought into their country; and Philip, watching from a height the order and lay-out of the Roman camp Publius Sulpicius Galba had pitched in his kingdom, made a similar remark. By which it appears how careful men ought to be of taking things on trust from common opinion, and that we ought to judge with the eye of reason, not by common report.

I long had a man living in my house who had spent ten or twelve years in the New World, in the part of it where Villegaignon landed and which he called Antarctic France. This discovery of so vast a country seems to me a thing of very great importance. I cannot be sure that no other will be made in the future, given how many wiser men than ourselves have been mistaken about this one. I am afraid our eyes are bigger than our bellies, and that we have more curiosity than capacity; we grasp at everything and end up holding only wind.

Plato has Solon tell a story he had heard from the priests of Sais in Egypt: that long ago, before the Flood, there was a great island called Atlantis, lying directly at the mouth of the Strait of Gibraltar, larger than Africa and Asia put together; that its kings ruled not only that island but also extended their dominion far into the continent — holding a portion of Africa as far as Egypt, and in Europe as far as Tuscany — and that they tried to push as well into Asia, subjugating all the nations bordering the Mediterranean as far as the Black Sea. To this end they overran all Spain, Gaul, and Italy, and pressed on into Greece, where the Athenians stopped them. But some time afterwards both the Athenians, and the islanders and their island, were swallowed by the Flood.
It is very likely that this enormous burst and inundation of water worked wonderful changes in the layout of the earth — as it is said that the sea then divided Sicily from Italy:
"Haec loca, vi quondam et vasta convulsa ruina, Dissiluisse ferunt, quum protenus utraque tellus Una foret"
["These lands, they say, formerly with violence and vast desolation convulsed, burst asunder, where erewhile were." — Aeneid, iii. 414.]
Cyprus from Syria, the island of Negropont from the continent of Boeotia; and elsewhere it joined lands that had been separate before, filling in the channel between them with sand and mud:
"Sterilisque diu palus, aptaque remis, Vicinas urbes alit, et grave sentit aratrum."
["That which was once a sterile marsh, and bore vessels on its bosom, now feeds neighbouring cities, and admits the plough." — Horace, De Arte Poetica, v. 65.]

But there is no real likelihood that this island was the New World so recently discovered: that almost touched Spain, and it would be an incredible feat of any flood to have thrown so prodigious a mass back more than twelve hundred leagues. Besides, our modern navigators have nearly established that it is no island but mainland, joined with the East Indies on one side, and with the lands under the two poles on the other; or, if it is separated from them, by so narrow a strait that it hardly deserves the name of an island on that account.

It seems that in this great body of the earth there are two sorts of motion, as in our own — one natural and the other feverish. When I think of the impression our river, the Dordogne, has made in my time on its right bank, how in twenty years it has gained so much ground and undermined the foundations of so many houses, I take it for an unusual agitation; for if it had always run that way, or were to do so in future, the look of the world would be wholly changed. But rivers alter their course, beating now against one bank, now the other, and sometimes keeping quietly to their channel. I am not speaking of sudden floods, the causes of which everyone understands. In Médoc, by the seashore, my brother, Sieur d'Arsac, sees an estate he owned there buried under the sands that the sea throws up before it; the tops of some houses are still to be seen, and his rents and lands have been turned into pitiful, barren scrub. The people of the place say that of late years the sea has been driving so hard against them that they have lost more than four leagues of land. These sands are her outriders, and we can now see great mounds of moving sand marching half a league ahead of her, taking the land as they go.

The other testimony from antiquity to which some would tie this discovery of the New World is in Aristotle — at any rate, if that little book on Marvellous Things Heard is his. He tells us there that certain Carthaginians, having crossed the Atlantic beyond the Strait of Gibraltar and sailed a very long time, at last came upon a great and fruitful island, all covered with wood and watered by several broad and deep rivers, lying far from any mainland; and that they, and others after them, drawn by the goodness and fertility of the soil, went there with their wives and children and began to plant a colony. But the Carthaginian senate, seeing their own people slowly diminishing in numbers, issued an express order on pain of death that no one should travel there, and drove out these new settlers — fearing, it is said, that in time the colony would so multiply as to supplant and ruin the home state. But this report of Aristotle's no more agrees with our new-found lands than the other.

The man I had was plain and ignorant, and so all the likelier to tell the truth — for your better-bred sort of men are sharper observers, true, and see more; but then they gloss over what they see, and, to give greater weight to what they tell you and win your belief, they cannot keep from tweaking the story a little. They never report things to you simply as they are, but as they appeared to them, or as they want them to appear to you; and to win a reputation for sound judgment, and to gain your trust, they are happy to help the case along with something more than is strictly true, of their own invention. What we need, in such a case, is either a man of unimpeachable honesty, or one so simple that he has nothing in him with which to dress up false stories and give them a colour of truth, and no axe to grind in fabricating. Mine was such a man; and besides, he has at various times brought me sailors and merchants who had made the same voyage at the same time. So I will content myself with his testimony, without bothering about what the cosmographers say. We should have topographers to map out for us the particular places they have actually been; but having had this advantage over us — of having seen the Holy Land — they think they have the right, naturally, to tell us stories about every other part of the world besides. I would have every man write down what he knows, and as much as he knows, but no more — and not just on this subject but on every other. For someone may have particular knowledge or experience of some river or fountain, who otherwise knows no more than anyone else, and yet, to get a circulation for his little hoard of learning, will undertake to write a whole book on physics. From this vice large mischiefs grow.

Now, to come back to my subject: from anything I can gather, there is nothing barbarous or savage about that nation, except that everyone calls barbarism whatever is not in use in his own country. Indeed, we have no other measure of truth and reason than the example and pattern of the opinions and customs of the place where we live: there is always the perfect religion, there the perfect government, there the most accomplished and proper usage of everything. They are savages in the same sense that we call fruits wild when they have grown of themselves, by nature's own ordinary course; whereas in truth we should rather call those wild whose nature we have changed by our artifice, and diverted from the common order. In the first sort the genuine, most useful, and natural virtues and properties are vigorous and lively, which in the others we have helped to corrupt by adjusting them to suit our corrupted palate. And yet even our taste can find a flavour and delicacy, beyond what we can match, in some of the fruits those countries produce without art or cultivation. It is not reasonable that art should win the prize over our great and powerful mother nature. We have so smothered the beauty and richness of her own work with the extra ornaments and graces of our invention that we have very nearly stifled her — yet in other places, where she shines in her own purity and proper lustre, she shames our vain and trivial efforts in the most striking way:
"Et veniunt hederae sponte sua melius; Surgit et in solis formosior arbutus antris; Et volucres nulls dulcius arte canunt."
["The ivy grows best spontaneously, the arbutus best in shady caves; and the wild notes of birds are sweeter than art can teach." — Propertius, i. 2, 10.]
Our best efforts cannot even imitate the nest of the least of birds — its make, its beauty, its convenience — or even a poor spider's web.
All things, Plato says, are produced either by nature, by chance, or by art; the greatest and finest by one or the other of the first two, the least and least perfect by the last.

These nations, then, seem to me barbarous only in this: that they have taken on so little stamp from human art and invention, and so are still very close to their original simplicity. The laws of nature still govern them, hardly contaminated by ours; and that in such purity that I am sometimes sorry we did not come to know them sooner, in those better ages when there were men more capable of judging them than we are. I am sorry that Lycurgus and Plato had no knowledge of them; for, to my mind, what we see now in these nations not only surpasses all the pictures with which the poets have decked out the golden age, and all their inventions in imagining a happy state of mankind, but it goes beyond the imagination and even the wish and longing of philosophy itself. So native and pure a simplicity as we see by experience to exist in them could never have entered the philosophers' minds, nor could they have believed that human society could be maintained with so little artifice and so little human patching. I would tell Plato that this is a nation with no sort of trade, no knowledge of letters, no science of numbers, no name for magistrate or political authority, no use of slavery, no riches or poverty, no contracts, no inheritances, no shares, no occupations except leisure, no respect of kinship beyond the common, no clothing, no agriculture, no metal, no use of corn or wine — the very words for lying, treachery, dissimulation, avarice, envy, slander, pardon, unheard of.
How short would he find his imaginary republic of this perfection?
"Viri a diis recentes."
["Men fresh from the gods." — Seneca, Ep., 90.]
"Hos natura modos primum dedit."
["These were the manners first taught by nature." — Virgil, Georgics, ii. 20.]

As for the rest, they live in a country that is very pleasant and temperate, so that, as my witnesses tell me, it is rare to hear of anyone falling ill, and they assure me they have never seen any of the natives palsied, bleary-eyed, toothless, or bent with age. The country lies along the seashore, fenced on the inland side by great high mountains, with a stretch of about a hundred leagues between. They have plenty of fish and meat, none of which look like ours, and they eat them with no cookery beyond plain boiling, roasting, and grilling. The first man to ride in there on a horse, though in earlier voyages he had become acquainted and familiar with them, frightened them so badly with his centaur appearance that they killed him with their arrows before they could make out who he was. Their houses are very long, big enough to hold two or three hundred people, made of the bark of tall trees, one end stuck in the ground and the trees leaning on each other at the top to support one another, like some of our barns, where the roof comes right down to the ground and serves as side walls too. They have wood so hard that they cut with it and make their swords from it, and grills from it to grill their meat. Their beds are of cotton, slung from the roof like our sailors' hammocks, every man with his own — for the wives sleep apart from their husbands. They rise with the sun, and as soon as they are up, eat for the whole day, since they have no further meals. They do not drink at meals — as Suidas reports of certain other peoples of the East who never drank with their food — but drink very often during the rest of the day, and sometimes to a rousing pitch. Their drink is made of a certain root and is the colour of our claret, and they only ever drink it lukewarm. It keeps no more than two or three days; it has a slightly sharp, brisk taste, is not at all heady, but very kind to the stomach; laxative to strangers but a pleasant beverage to those used to it. Instead of bread they use a certain white compound, like coriander seeds; I have tasted it — the flavour is sweet and a little bland. The whole day is spent in dancing. The young men go off to hunt wild beasts with bows and arrows; meanwhile some of the women are busy heating their drink, which is their chief occupation. One of their old men, in the morning before they begin to eat, preaches to the whole household, walking from one end of the house to the other and repeating the same sentence over and over until he has completed the round — for their houses are at least a hundred yards long. Valour against their enemies and love toward their wives are the two heads of his sermon, never failing to remind them, in closing, that it is their wives who give them their drink warm and well-seasoned. The shape of their beds, ropes, swords, the wooden bracelets they tie around their wrists when they go to fight, and the great canes hollowed out at one end, by whose sound they keep the cadence of their dances, are to be seen in several places, and among them at my house. They shave themselves all over, and much more neatly than we do, with no razor but one of wood or stone. They believe in the immortality of the soul, and that those who have deserved well of the gods are lodged in that part of heaven where the sun rises, and the damned in the west.

They have I do not know what kind of priests and prophets, who very rarely appear in public, living up in the mountains. When one of them arrives there is a great feast and a solemn assembly of several villages — each house, as I have described, makes a village, and they are about a French league apart. This prophet speaks publicly to the people, urging them to virtue and duty; but all their ethics come down to two articles: resoluteness in war, and devotion to their wives. He also prophesies to them the events to come and the outcomes they may expect from their enterprises, and pushes them toward war or away from it. But he had better look out: if he fails in his prediction, and anything turns out otherwise than he foretold, he is hacked into a thousand pieces if he is caught, and condemned as a false prophet. For that reason, any of them who has been wrong once is heard from no more.

Divination is a gift of God, and so to abuse it ought to be a punishable imposture. Among the Scythians, when their diviners failed to deliver what they had promised, they were bound hand and foot, laid on carts loaded with brushwood and faggots, drawn along by oxen, and burned alive. Those who deal only with matters within the reach of human capacity are excusable in doing the best they can. But those others, who come to swindle us with claims of an extraordinary faculty beyond our understanding — ought they not to be punished when they fail to make good their promise, and for the rashness of their imposture?

They are continually at war with the nations who live further inland, beyond their mountains, to which they go naked, with no other weapons than their bows and wooden swords, shaped at one end like the head of our javelins. The obstinacy of their battles is something wonderful, and they never end without much loss of blood — for as for running away, they do not know what that is. Each one brings home, for a trophy, the head of an enemy he has killed, and fixes it over the door of his house. After treating their prisoners very well for a long time, and giving them every delicacy they can think of, the man to whom the prisoner belongs invites a great gathering of his friends. When they are all assembled, he ties a rope to one of the prisoner's arms, holding the other end himself at a distance out of his reach, and gives his closest friend the other arm to hold in the same way; and then the two of them, in front of the whole assembly, dispatch the prisoner with their swords. After that they roast him, eat him among themselves, and send some morsels to absent friends. They do not do this, as some have supposed, for nourishment — as the Scythians anciently did — but as the ultimate token of revenge. This appears from the following: having seen that the Portuguese, who were allied to their enemies, inflicted a different sort of death on prisoners they took — burying them up to the waist, shooting arrows at the upper part until it bristled with them, and then hanging them — they assumed that these people from another world, who had spread the knowledge of many vices to their neighbours and were far greater masters of every sort of mischief than they were, must have a reason for adopting this kind of revenge, and that it must be more painful than their own; so they began to drop their old way and follow this one. I am not so much sorry that we should note the barbarous horror of so cruel a deed, as that, while we see their faults so plainly, we are so blind to our own. I take it that there is more barbarity in eating a man alive than in eating him dead; in tearing apart by racks and torments a body still in full sensation; in roasting it by degrees, in having it bitten and worried to death by dogs and pigs (as we have not only read about, but lately seen — not between sworn and mortal enemies, but between neighbours and fellow-citizens, and, what is worse, under the colour of piety and religion) — than to roast and eat him after he is dead.

Chrysippus and Zeno, the two heads of the Stoic school, thought there was no harm in using our dead bodies in whatever way we needed, even for food — as our own ancestors did, when, besieged by Caesar in the city of Alesia, they decided to keep themselves alive during the siege on the bodies of their old men, women, and others unfit to bear arms.
"Vascones, ut fama est, alimentis talibus usi Produxere animas."
["It is said the Gascons with such meats appeased their hunger." — Juvenal, Sat., xv. 93.]

And our physicians make no bones about putting it to all sorts of uses, applying it either outwardly or giving it inwardly, for the health of the patient. But no opinion has ever been so out of bounds as to excuse treachery, disloyalty, tyranny, and cruelty — which are our familiar vices. So we may indeed call these people barbarous as judged by the rules of reason, but not as judged against ourselves, who outdo them in every kind of barbarity. Their wars are throughout noble and generous, and have as much excuse and fair pretext as that human plague is capable of: their sole motive is the rivalry of valour. Their disputes are not over new territory — what they already have is so fruitful by nature that it supplies them, without labour or worry, with everything they need in such abundance that they have no use for enlarging their borders. They are still at that happy stage where they want only as much as their natural needs require; everything beyond that is, for them, superfluous. Men of the same age commonly call one another brothers, the younger ones children, and the old men are fathers to all. The old leave their goods to their heirs in common possession, without any division or any other title than what nature gives her creatures in bringing them into the world. If their neighbours cross the mountains to attack them and win the day, all the victors gain is glory and the advantage of having shown themselves the better in valour and virtue. They never meddle with the goods of the conquered, but go straight home to their own country, where they want for nothing they need — and not for that greatest of goods either, the knowledge of how to enjoy their condition happily and be content. The other side, in turn, does the same. They demand no other ransom of their prisoners than the acknowledgment that they have been defeated; but you will not find one in a generation who will not rather choose to die than make such a confession, or in any word or look fall short of the full grandeur of an undefeated courage. There is not one of them who would not rather be killed and eaten than so much as open his mouth to plead that he might not be. Their captors treat them with all liberality and freedom, to make their lives that much dearer to them — but frequently bring up the subject of their approaching death, the torments they are to suffer, the preparations being made for them, the carving up of their limbs, and the feast at which their carcass will be the only dish. All this they do for one end only: to wring some soft or submissive word from them, or so to frighten them as to make them run off, in order to gain the advantage of having scared them and shaken their constancy. And in fact, if you look at it rightly, that is the only point on which true victory turns:
"Victoria nulla est, Quam quae confessor animo quoque subjugat hostes."
["No victory is complete which the conquered do not admit to be so." — Claudian, De Sexto Consulatu Honorii, v. 248.]

The Hungarians, a very warlike people, never push further than reducing the enemy to surrender; once that confession has been wrung from them, they let them go without injury or ransom — except, at most, to bind them by their word never to take up arms against them again. We have plenty of advantages over our enemies that are borrowed, not really our own. To have stronger arms and legs is a porter's quality, not the effect of virtue; to draw oneself up in formation is a dead, corporeal quality; it is a turn of fortune that makes an enemy stumble or dazzles him with the sun; it is a trick of science and craft, possible even in a base man, to be a good fencer. The worth and value of a man lies in the heart and in the will: there is his real honour. Valour is steadiness, not of legs and arms, but of courage and soul; it does not consist in the goodness of our horse or our weapons, but in our own. He who stays firm in his courage —
"Si succiderit, de genu pugnat"
["If his legs fail him, he fights on his knees." — Seneca, De Providentia, c. 2.]

— he who gives up nothing of his self-possession in the face of imminent death, who dying still throws his enemy a fierce and disdainful look, is overcome not by us but by fortune; he is killed, not conquered. The most valiant are sometimes the most unfortunate. There are defeats more triumphant than victories. Those four sister victories — the fairest the sun ever looked on, of Salamis, Plataea, Mycale, and Sicily — never dared to set their united glory against the single glory of the rout of King Leonidas and his men at the pass of Thermopylae. Who ever ran with a more glorious purpose, a higher ambition, toward winning a battle than Captain Iscolas did toward the certain loss of one? Who could have come up with a more subtle device to secure his own safety than he found to assure his own destruction? He was sent to defend a certain pass of the Peloponnese against the Arcadians; finding it utterly impossible, given the lie of the ground and the imbalance of forces, and seeing that all who faced the enemy must inevitably be left dead on the spot, yet judging it unworthy of his own virtue and magnanimity, and of the Lacedaemonian name, to fail in any part of his duty, he chose a middle course between those two extremes. He saved the youngest and fittest of his men for the service and defence of their country and sent them back; with the rest, whose loss would be of less moment, he resolved to hold the pass and, by their deaths, make the enemy pay as dearly as possible for getting through. And so it fell out: surrounded on all sides by the Arcadians, he and his men, after killing a great many of the enemy, were cut to pieces. Is there a single trophy dedicated to the conquerors that was not far more due to those who lost? The part of true conquering lies in the encounter, not in the coming out the other side; the honour of valour consists in fighting, not in subduing.

But to come back to my story: these prisoners are so far from showing the least weakness, in spite of all the terrors held up to them, that, on the contrary, during the two or three months they are kept they always wear a cheerful look, urge their captors to hurry up and put them to the test, defy them, jeer at them, taunt them with cowardice, and with the number of battles they have lost against their compatriots. I have a song made by one of these prisoners, in which he tells them to "come all and dine on him, and welcome, for in him they will also be eating their own fathers and grandfathers, whose flesh has gone to feed and nourish him. These muscles," he says, "this flesh and these veins, are your own: poor silly souls that you are, you little think that the substance of your ancestors' limbs is still here; pay attention to what you eat, and you will find in it the taste of your own flesh." In that song there is a touch of invention that has nothing barbarous about it. Those who paint these people dying in this manner show the prisoner spitting in the faces of his executioners and making wry mouths at them. And it is quite certain that to the very last gasp they never stop defying and braving them in word and gesture. In plain truth, these men are indeed savages compared with us; either they must be wholly so, or else we are; for there is a vast difference between their manners and ours.

The men there have several wives, and the more wives the higher their reputation for valour. And it is one very remarkable feature of their marriages that the same jealousy our wives use to keep us from the friendship and intimacy of other women, theirs use to further their husbands' desires and to procure them many partners. Above all things concerned for their husbands' honour, they make it their chief care to seek out and bring in as many companions as they can, since this is held to be evidence of their husband's worth. Most of our ladies will cry out that this is monstrous; in truth, it is not so, but a truly matrimonial virtue of the highest order. In the Bible, Sarah, with Leah and Rachel, the two wives of Jacob, gave the most beautiful of their handmaids to their husbands; Livia, in her own interest, indulged Augustus's passions for other women; and the wife of King Deiotarus, Stratonice, not only gave up a beautiful young maid in her service to her husband's embraces, but carefully brought up the children he had by her and helped them on to the succession of their father's crown.

And lest it be supposed that all this is done out of a simple, servile attachment to common custom, or by some authoritative impression of ancient practice, with no judgment or reasoning behind it — out of a soul too dull to think of anything else — I should give you a few touches of their understanding. Besides what I have just quoted of one of their war songs, I have another, a love song, that begins like this:

"Stay, adder, stay, so that by your pattern my sister may draw the design and work of a rich ribbon, which I may give to my beloved; and so your beauty and the exquisite order of your scales shall be preferred forever above all other serpents."

The first couplet — "Stay, adder," and so on — is the refrain of the song. Now I have spent enough time with poetry to be a judge of this much: that not only is there nothing barbarous in this invention, but it is, moreover, thoroughly Anacreontic. I might add that their language is soft, with a pleasing accent, and something close to Greek in its endings.

Three of these people, not foreseeing how dear a knowledge of the corruptions of this part of the world would one day cost their happiness and peace of mind — nor that their dealings with us are leading, as I take them to be, straight to their ruin (poor wretches, to let themselves be taken in by the desire for novelty, leaving the serenity of their own sky to come so far to gape at ours!) — were at Rouen when the late King Charles IX was there. The king himself talked with them a good while; they were shown our fashions, our pomp, the shape of a great city. Afterwards someone asked their opinion, wanting to know what among all the things they had seen they thought most worth admiring. To which they answered three things — of which I have forgotten the third, and am sorry for it, but two I still remember. They said, first, that they thought it very strange that so many tall men, bearded, strong, well-armed, who stood about the king (probably they meant the Swiss Guard), should submit to obeying a child, and not rather pick out one of their own number to command. Secondly (they have a way of speaking in their language by which they call men the halves of one another) they had noticed that there were among us men full and crammed with every sort of good, while their other halves were begging at their doors, lean and half-starved with hunger and poverty; and they thought it strange that these needy halves were able to bear such inequality and injustice, and did not take the others by the throat or set fire to their houses.

I talked with one of them for a good while, but I had so poor an interpreter, and one so muddled by his own ignorance to catch my meaning, that I could get nothing of much weight out of him. Asking what advantage he got from the rank he held among his own people (for he was a captain, and our sailors called him king), he told me: to march at the head of them to war. Asking him further how many men followed him, he showed me a stretch of ground to signify as many as could march on such a piece — perhaps four or five thousand men. Asking whether his authority lapsed with the war, he told me this much remained: that when he went to visit the villages under him, they cleared paths for him through the thick of the woods, so that he could pass at his ease. All this does not sound at all bad — and the last detail is not bad at all, considering they wear no breeches.
